hits.name: Corey Ganim
hits.text:
A college student quoted a private equity CEO $25,000/month for AI consulting, hoping the CEO would counter at $10,000.

To his surprise the CEO was genuinely interested in the $25K offer.

James Larson and his 2 co-founders (also both in college) were on that call trying not to smile.

They ended up settling at $15K/month for the first 6 months. They future paced the CEO's expectations by mentioning a maintenance plan of at least $5K/month once the engagement ends.

James is 23 and still a full-time student at BYU.

Here's his exact system you can copy:

THE WAY IN

He asked his network for intros to companies doing $10M+. Then he asked those owners for advice, NOT A SALES CALL. Most CEOs are willing to give ambitious young people advice, and many of those casual conversations turn into sales conversations.

THE ASSESSMENT

They charged for it from day 1. They started at $1,000 then recently closed one at $5,000.

They survey every department head before they do the actual assessment so they begin the assessment already knowing their pain points and software. Then they record a 30-minute call with each one and ask for real examples of their work.

THE MAP

James and his co-founders rank every workflow by ROI, using the numbers their client gave them. This client got 19 workflows and a conservative estimate of $255K to $285K back in year one.

THE DEMO

They build working demos on their clients' real documents and show the whole C-suite on one call. This is what got the room excited.

THE PRICE

They like to quote 3 tiers at prices higher than feels comfortable.

During our interview I advised James to take the price he's comfortable with, double it, and let them negotiate down from there.

The whole sales cycle for this $15K/month deal took about 6 weeks. They have a ton of similar deals in the pipeline and the future is bright for these guys!

James screen shared his entire business model on the Build With AI podcast.

Full video below.

https://t.co/CaRCHjosqg

(Also available on the Build With AI podcast wherever you get your pods)

hits.name: Danny Postma
hits.text:
I've been listening to a few episodes now and it's crazy to me how most founders have no clue who their customers are.

You can't fix your landing page, ads or roadmap until you know who they're for.

I've automated most of this at HeadshotPro

Here's my setup

> 1. Ask during onboarding, not after

New teams answer 5 quick questions while setting up:

• What's your role?
• Where will the photos go?
• When will you need more?
• What would you do without us?
• Which feature would solve a problem for you?

It's part of setup, not a popup.

So most people actually answer.

> 2. Read every sales email

Agents pull the first message from every inbound lead and tag why they reached out.

It's almost never what you'd guess.

> 3. Track everything in PostHog

Every click, upload, edit and purchase is an event.

So we don't just know what people say they'll do.

We see what they actually do in the product.

> 4. Check what they say against what they pay

We match every survey answer to their PostHog events and payment data.

The people who answer your surveys the most are often not the ones paying you the most.

> 5. Turn it into an ICP

Agents put everything into one doc using the SPICED framework:

• Situation: what's true before they find you
• Pain: the problem, in their own words
• Impact: what changes once it's solved
• Critical event: what makes them buy now
• Decision: who signs up, who approves, what they check

Then we split customers by pain, not by industry or company size.

Every pain gets its own message, objection and landing page angle.

We also note who finds you (the champion) and who pays (the approver).

Plus a checklist of good-fit and bad-fit signals.

That doc runs our landing pages, ads, sales replies and roadmap.

> 6. Keep it running

New answers come in every day.

So the ICP never goes stale.

No calls. No guessing.

Ask at the right moment and check it against who actually pays.

Yesterday, while at my in-laws, I shot a prompt to Amp.

In essence, I said that hey, the 10-year anniversary of https://t.co/arW0hnVET0 is coming up. I want that site and https://t.co/RN9xXOzhON to be on modern foundations. (I used Ruby & Middleman back in 2016, no CSS framework.)

Didn't really specify anything, except that it should be a "modern stack" and that we should also collect some testimonials because the books have become niche classics.

It worked for 52min, rebuilt both pages on top of Astro, went out and found great testimonials on HackerNews, Goodreads, etc.

Our Signal Stack.

It's a short list of sources Claude Code/Codex reads every week so that we're always up to date on the market, our competitors, trends, etc.

Here are the sources we use + the setup:

Customers:

-Where our buyers talk about the problems we solve
-Their words
-Their venues
-Their tone

Competitors

-5-10 competitors or substitutes
-What they're shipping
-What they're charging
-What they're hiring for

Market

-Regulatory shifts
-Sector economics
-Events that change what buyers prioritize

Internal

-CRM
-Fathom call transcripts
-Slack
-Customer feedback

Every source has to pass 3 tests:

-Specific: covers our problem space, not "AI" generally
-Recent: not old/outdated
-Decision-relevant: we can make informed decisions based on the data

The setup:

1) We have Claude read our business context files
2) We had it interview us about our market (10 questions)
3) It then sorts our sources into 4 buckets, each with a one-line "why this exists"
4) DON'T SKIP THIS STEP: It cuts every source without a "why"
5) We schedule a brief for Monday at 8am
6) It gets a monthly check for dead URLs, drifted sources, and duplicates

Highly recommend you set this up for yourself, also something good to set up for clients for an additional fee or just a value-add on top of your existing service(s).

hits.name: Hamel Husain
hits.text:
Should you rely on public benchmark scores when choosing a model? @VikParuchuri argues "no" in this talk.

To illustrate this, he shows specific problems found in popular OCR benchmarks:

ParseBench:

• A test expects 310 gigawatts of solar-panel capacity when the correct value is 303.  Additionally, 73% of its chart tests ask for values that aren't printed on the chart. (4:51)

• A test requires "Parish Priest:" to be bold even though those words aren't bold in the source document. (15:33)

• The scorer fails to recognize heading tags placed on separate lines. (16:15)

• dots.mocr ranks last among six models even though it beats the first-ranked model on content and tables.  This is an example of how overall benchmark score can hide important differences in model capabilities. (14:48)

olmOCR-bench:

• A model correctly preserves a line break in a document and gets penalized for it. (10:30)

• A test expects "Republican Party" when a document says "Republican party". Copying the capitalization correctly makes the model fail. (10:49)

• A 700-line postprocessor that rewrites model output adds 1 to 2 points, more than many gaps between models. (12:12)

OmniDocBench:

• This benchmark uses edit distance, which penalizes a correct table written in HTML more heavily than a wrong number in Markdown. So the format matters more than the answer! (6:58)

This is just the tip of the iceberg, the video contains more examples.

Chapters:

0:00 Choosing a model when every vendor claims to be #1
1:54 How OCR benchmark scores improve without better OCR
5:30 Metric design and tests that reject correct answers
11:33 Postprocessing, saturation, and misleading model rankings
12:40 How to slice benchmarks by your task and check for bias
16:53 How to build fair tests with verified answers and consistent scoring
19:05 How to test OCR models on your own documents
24:10 Benchmark marketing, private evals, and how to choose a model
